task.goal: Help eight children explain why the Moon can appear in different shapes without confusing phases with Earth's shadow.
hard_constraints: Use one lamp and foam balls indoors; never ask children to stare into the lamp.
Do not teach that a lunar eclipse causes ordinary monthly phases.
Fit a 25-minute session and check understanding with a new Sun-Earth-Moon position.
task.available_resources: Lamp, foam balls, darkened room and drawing cards.
task.expected_result: A safe visual lesson and a transfer question.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Be Earth: watch the illuminated half change its appearance
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Main mechanism: children directly compare a ball’s consistently illuminated half with the changing fraction visible from their own viewpoint. Their heads represent Earth; the lamp represents the Sun. Changing viewing geometry changes the apparent shape without changing which half receives light.

Before children enter, place the lamp securely at adult-controlled height, with its hot parts and cable out of reach. Keep enough room light for safe movement. Establish: look at the foam ball, never into the lamp; if looking toward the lamp would be necessary, skip that position. Assume the foam balls are opaque and the lamp produces a visible light-dark boundary; inspect this beforehand.

Use 0–3 minutes for safety and initial explanations. During minutes 3–6, illuminate one ball and show that approximately half its surface receives direct light. During minutes 6–14, work with four pairs: one child observes while the partner slowly moves a ball around the observer, then swap. Keep balls above head level where necessary so heads do not cast shadows onto them. Use side and behind-the-observer positions; omit the directly lampward position. Children describe or draw how much of the bright half they see.

During minutes 14–19, connect drawings: the Moon remains round, sunlight illuminates roughly half, and Earth observers see different portions of that half. Earth's shadow causes a lunar eclipse only during special alignments; it does not explain ordinary phases.

This needs no additional equipment, but nearby lamp light and imperfect ball positioning make exact phase shapes approximate.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Use minutes 19–25 for individual transfer checks. Move the lamp to a different side of the room and choose a previously unused, oblique ball position. Before demonstrating, each child draws the expected bright portion as viewed from Earth and explains why. Then reveal the ball from that viewpoint. Compare these explanations with each child's opening explanation. A correct drawing alone is insufficient: ask whether Earth's shadow must touch the ball. Persistent shadow explanations, or inability to predict the changed position despite recalling familiar drawings, would show that the lesson has not achieved transfer.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Test two explanations: changing viewpoint or Earth's shadow?
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Main mechanism: children distinguish competing explanations by making predictions and deliberately changing whether an Earth shadow reaches the Moon model. This makes the absence of Earth's shadow observable rather than merely asserted.

Assume at least two opaque foam balls are available and a preliminary inspection confirms that one can cast a recognizable shadow on another. The lamp represents the Sun, one ball Earth, and another the Moon. The teacher controls the lamp and all model movement. Children stand in a viewing area facing away from the lamp, looking only toward the balls; no one looks along a sightline into the light source. Keep the lamp stable, its cable clear, and sufficient ambient light for safe movement.

Minutes 0–4: explain safety and collect initial drawings. Minutes 4–8: show a Moon ball illuminated from the side, with the Earth ball well clear of the light path. Children notice a partly bright appearance even though Earth casts no shadow onto it. Ask what each proposed explanation predicts.

Minutes 8–14: move the Earth ball through and then out of the lamp-to-Moon light path while holding the Moon fixed. Children compare the temporary cast shadow with the persistent division between the Moon's day and night sides. Name the shadow event as an eclipse model, not an ordinary monthly phase.

Minutes 14–20: place the Earth ball outside that shadow-producing alignment. Children view the Moon from near Earth's position while the teacher changes the Moon's location, drawing the visible illuminated portion on cards. Explain that phases result from seeing different amounts of the sunlit half.

The model exaggerates sizes and eclipse frequency. Explicitly explain that the real Moon's tilted orbit usually keeps it outside Earth's shadow.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: During minutes 20–25, give each child a new oblique Sun-Earth-Moon arrangement, with Earth clearly outside the lamp-to-Moon light path. Ask for a predicted drawing from Earth's viewpoint and an explanation of whether a phase can occur without Earth's shadow. Reveal the model view afterward. Compare with the initial drawings and explanations, using the simple alternative of merely naming a memorized phase as the comparator. If children can identify the staged eclipse but still require Earth's shadow to explain the new ordinary phase, the contrast has failed; correct it by tracing the unobstructed light path and inspecting the Moon ball again.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Combine two maps: what sunlight reaches and what Earth can see
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Main mechanism: children construct a phase by combining two separate pieces of information: which half of the Moon receives sunlight, and which half faces Earth. This uses a drawing prediction before observation, making the overlap of those halves the explanation.

Needs: one lamp, one opaque foam ball, drawing cards and a way to draw on them. Assume the ball shows a clear light-dark boundary; inspect this beforehand. An adult controls the stable lamp, keeps its cable and hot parts inaccessible, and maintains enough room light for movement. Children look only at the ball and cards, never into the lamp. Use viewing positions with the lamp behind or beside them.

Minutes 0–4: introduce safety and collect each child's explanation of a partly bright Moon. Minutes 4–8: illuminate the ball from the side. Establish that it remains round and approximately half receives direct light. Explain that Earth's shadow is unnecessary here; a lunar eclipse is a separate event requiring special alignment.

Minutes 8–16: divide eight children into four pairs. Give each pair a top-down drawing showing Sun, Earth and Moon. One child draws the Moon's half facing the Sun; the other identifies its half facing Earth. Together they identify the surface belonging to both halves and predict whether Earth sees little, half or most of the sunlit side. Model one example first. The adult then positions the ball for inspection from Earth's direction, keeping everyone out of the light path. Swap roles for another arrangement.

Minutes 16–20: pairs explain why the unlit portion is the Moon's night side, rather than Earth's shadow. A top-down overlap indicates the amount visible, but does not itself draw the exact curved appearance; use the ball to connect these representations. Spatial drawing demands may limit younger children's success.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Minutes 20–25: give each child a new arrangement with sunlight coming from a different direction on the card and the Moon at an unfamiliar oblique position. Before revealing the ball, ask them to identify the Sun-facing half, the Earth-facing half, and predict little, half or most illuminated appearance. Ask whether Earth must block any sunlight. Compare this with a simple phase-name question: naming a phase without correctly identifying both halves does not demonstrate the mechanism. Incorrect overlap predictions or continued shadow explanations would show that the card method needs further support. Use the final minute to inspect the corresponding ball view and correct the explanation.

EXPAND.title: Build a phase using two separate rules: lit and visible
EXPAND.proposal:
The mechanism is a constructive reasoning procedure: children separately identify which Moon surface receives sunlight and which surface faces Earth, then combine those conditions. This addresses a gap in the observation lessons: seeing a convincing shape does not necessarily explain how that shape follows from the geometry.

Before the session, the teacher checks that the lamp produces a clear boundary on an opaque foam ball. Secure the lamp and cable, keep hot parts inaccessible, and retain enough ambient light for movement. Arrange every viewing position so children look toward the ball with the lamp to their side or behind them; omit any position requiring a lampward gaze.

Minutes 0–4: collect initial explanations and establish safety. Minutes 4–8: illuminate a ball and explain that sunlight reaches approximately half its surface. Earth does not need to block any light for the opposite half to be dark.

Minutes 8–16: eight children work in four pairs using drawing cards. On a top-view circle representing the Moon, they draw the lamp direction and identify the half facing it. On a second drawing of the same arrangement, they identify the half facing an Earth ball. They then point to the surface satisfying both rules: illuminated and visible from Earth. The teacher connects that shared surface to the appearance of the real ball viewed from near Earth's position. Swap partners' roles.

Minutes 16–20: repeat with another safe arrangement and have children explain the two rules without phase names. State explicitly that Earth's cast shadow produces a lunar eclipse in special alignments; ordinary phases follow these visibility rules.

This requires only the lamp, balls and drawable cards. The main uncertainty is whether the children can interpret top views; these drawings establish which surface qualifies, but do not by themselves reproduce its curved appearance.
EXPAND.experiment: Minutes 20–25: the teacher gives every child a previously unused oblique Sun–Earth–Moon arrangement. Each predicts the appearance and explains both conditions before inspecting the ball. For a first trial, give four children the construction procedure and four an equal-time direct-view demonstration, then use the same transfer question. Record independent causal explanations and time spent resolving diagram confusion. Stop the diagram activity if children cannot locate Earth-facing and lamp-facing halves after one guided retry; recover with direct inspection. No increase in correct explanations, or substantially greater confusion, would argue against the added procedure.

EXPAND.title: Solve the model backward from a phase card
EXPAND.proposal:
The mechanism is inverse construction with immediate feedback: children must build a geometry that explains an observed appearance. Choosing and defending a position makes their causal model actionable, exposing explanations that merely repeat what an adult demonstrated.

The teacher first checks that the foam balls show a visible light-dark boundary. Secure the lamp, protect its hot parts and cable, and keep enough room light for safe movement. Establish a fixed Earth observation station with the lamp behind or beside observers. Only use Moon positions visible from that station without looking toward the lamp. The teacher controls all equipment; children propose positions from the safe viewing area.

Minutes 0–4: establish safety and collect an initial explanation. Minutes 4–8: use one ball to show its illuminated and unilluminated halves. Explain that the Moon stays round, and Earth sees some portion of the sunlit half. Earth's shadow is involved in lunar eclipses, not ordinary monthly phases.

Minutes 8–17: form four pairs. Give each pair a drawing-card target showing a half-lit or mostly lit Moon. Each pair proposes where the teacher should place the Moon ball relative to the fixed Earth station and lamp, and predicts why it will match. Place the ball as requested, let the pair inspect it, and allow one revision. Other pairs silently predict whether each placement will work before the reveal. Use broad illuminated fractions rather than demanding exact drawn curves.

Minutes 17–20: pairs explain a successful placement using an unobstructed light path and the portion visible from Earth. A failed placement becomes a recovery opportunity: identify whether the error concerns illumination or Earth's viewing direction, then revise that relationship.

Prerequisites are drawable cards and enough safe space for several distinct positions. Multiple placements can produce similar appearances, so accept any physically valid solution. Spatial reasoning demands may outweigh the benefit for younger children.
EXPAND.experiment: Minutes 20–25: use a new oblique arrangement and ask all eight children individually to draw and explain the appearance before revealing it. For a bounded first trial, the teacher gives two pairs inverse-construction turns and two pairs equal-time teacher-led demonstrations, with both groups seeing comparable positions. Compare transfer explanations, dependence on prompts, and time needed to achieve a usable placement. Stop a pair's search after one unsuccessful revision and provide a worked explanation. If construction yields no better independent explanations while increasing frustration or reducing completion, prefer the simpler demonstration. This small comparison is exploratory, not evidence of a reliable effect.

EXPAND.title: Validated pair observations with a quick recovery demonstration
EXPAND.proposal:
Upgrade of “Be Earth: watch the illuminated half change its appearance.” Preserve direct observation: the lamp lights approximately half a round Moon ball, while its position changes how much of that half an Earth observer sees. The added action is a teacher acceptance check before each pair works independently; the original above-head instruction alone may leave children observing accidental head or hand shadows.

Before class, the teacher checks that the balls show a clear light-dark boundary, secures the lamp and cable, and keeps hot parts inaccessible. Retain enough ambient light for movement. Children look only at balls; omit every position requiring a gaze toward the lamp. This assumes enough balls for four pairs and adequate space; otherwise use one teacher-held ball with four pairs taking observation turns.

Minutes 0–3: establish safety and collect initial explanations. Minutes 3–6: show the illuminated half. Minutes 6–14: four pairs alternate observer and ball-holder roles. Before accepting a pair's setup, the teacher inspects its view and asks the holder to raise or shift the ball slightly. If an apparent dark patch disappears when the observer's head or holder's hand clears the light path, reset the setup. Accept only a position with a stable day-night boundary and unobstructed illumination. Allow one reset, then bring that pair to the teacher's verified demonstration position; do not spend the session troubleshooting. After an interruption or role swap, the holder waits for the observer to confirm the verified position before continuing.

Minutes 14–19: children connect their drawings to the explanation: the Moon stays round, sunlight illuminates roughly half, and Earth sees varying portions of that half. Earth's shadow can cause a lunar eclipse in special alignments; it does not cause ordinary monthly phases. Use broad fractions because a nearby lamp and oversized models distort exact shapes.

The check costs teacher attention but may prevent misleading observations from becoming explanations. Its value is uncertain until tried.
EXPAND.experiment:
The teacher runs one 25-minute session, recording how many pairs need a reset or the shared demonstration. Stop independent pair work if two pairs still show unwanted shadows after one reset each; finish with the verified teacher-held model within the same timetable.

During minutes 19–25, place the Moon at a previously unused oblique position, outside Earth's shadow and safely visible without looking toward the lamp. Each of the eight children independently draws the expected bright portion and explains why before viewing it. Ask whether Earth's shadow must reach the Moon. Count explanations that connect illumination and Earth’s viewpoint, rather than accepting a phase name or drawing alone. Compare these with opening explanations. Against the source's unverified pair activity, inspect both transfer understanding and the added checking time; this first trial cannot establish superiority without a comparable source session.

EXPAND.title: Make the shadow comparison conditional on a clear demonstration
EXPAND.proposal:
Upgrade of “Test two explanations: changing viewpoint or Earth's shadow?” Preserve its mechanism: use a controlled change in Earth's obstruction to distinguish a cast shadow from the Moon's ordinary unilluminated side. The changed procedure gives the teacher a concrete fallback when the staged eclipse is visually ambiguous, instead of making a recognizable cast shadow a prerequisite for the entire lesson.

Before class, the teacher secures the lamp, cable and hot parts, retains safe ambient light, and checks two opaque foam balls. All children view the balls with the lamp beside or behind them; no child looks into the lamp. From the intended viewing position, hold the Moon fixed and move the Earth ball into and out of the light path. Accept the eclipse demonstration only if the teacher can clearly distinguish an additional moving shadow from the existing day-night boundary on two successive passes. If not, omit the staged eclipse and use the Earth-removal procedure below. Model sizes are exaggerated, and successful staging does not represent eclipse frequency.

Minutes 0–4: safety and initial explanations. Minutes 4–8: show a partly bright Moon ball with the Earth ball clear of the light path. Minutes 8–13: if the precheck passed, move Earth into and out of alignment while Moon, lamp and viewing position stay fixed. Ask children to point to the additional shadow. If they cannot distinguish it after one repeat, stop staging it. Remove the Earth ball entirely while retaining the same observation point: the partly bright appearance remains even though the Earth model cannot block the light. Explain that the Moon's unlit side faces away from the lamp. State that real lunar eclipses involve Earth's shadow, while ordinary phases do not; the Moon's tilted orbit usually avoids that shadow.

Minutes 13–20: with Earth out of the light path, change Moon position and let four pairs take turns observing from near Earth's marked location, represented by a drawing card. Children draw and explain the visible illuminated portion. The teacher owns all model movement and restores the last verified arrangement after any interruption.

This fallback retains the causal comparison when shadow quality fails, at the cost of a less vivid eclipse example. It requires two balls and a visible ordinary light-dark boundary; if that boundary is unclear, use the balls as position markers and teach from drawing cards, acknowledging that the physical appearance could not be verified.
EXPAND.experiment:
The teacher's bounded first trial includes the precheck and one session. Stop the eclipse segment after one unsuccessful classroom repeat, immediately using Earth removal; do not extend the 25 minutes.

Minutes 20–25: present a new oblique Sun–Earth–Moon position with Earth outside the lamp-to-Moon light path. Every child predicts and draws the appearance from Earth before inspecting it, then explains whether an Earth shadow is necessary. Record causal explanations, remaining shadow claims, and minutes spent clarifying the staged eclipse. Compare with opening explanations. Relative to the source procedure, assess whether the fallback preserves transfer while reducing time lost to ambiguous shadows. If children still attribute phases to Earth's shadow, finish by removing Earth again and asking them to explain the persisting dark portion. This is corrective evidence, not proof that the lesson has succeeded.
